title: Distributing Quantum Circuits Using Pre-Distributed Entanglement Pairs over Quantum Networks
authors: Yukun Yang, Ranjani G. Sundaram, Himanshu Gupta
abstract: Distributing quantum circuits across a network of quantum devices is a recent approach to improve the scalability of quantum computation. Entangled pairs of qubits distributed across network nodes are used as a communication resource for executing inter-node (remote) gates. However, establishing these entanglement pairs incurs significant latency, and doing so during the circuit's execution may lead to the decoherence of logical qubits. Instead, it may be beneficial to distribute certain entanglement pairs before the circuit is executed. Thus, we consider the problem of distributing a quantum circuit across a quantum network containing some pre-distributed entanglement pairs and seek to minimize the execution time of the circuit.   We address this problem in three steps. First, given the quantum network and (optionally) a probability distribution over training circuits, we determine a set of pre-distributed entanglement pairs under a specified budget. Second, we compute a qubit-to-memory allocation that minimizes the expected execution time given these pre-distributed resources. Finally, we identify any additional entanglement pairs required during execution, generate them concurrently, and execute the circuit gates. We evaluate our methods on a broad range of benchmark circuits.
summary: This work proposes a framework to optimize quantum circuit execution across distributed quantum networks by proactively distributing entanglement pairs before computation begins. It formulates this as a joint optimization problem involving resource allocation and qubit placement. The methodology demonstrates that combining circuit-aware training for EPs with optimal qubit mapping significantly reduces overall execution time compared to simpler strategies.
main_problem: The paper addresses minimizing the execution time of a quantum circuit distributed across a quantum network by strategically utilizing pre-distributed entanglement pairs (EPs).
main_result: The joint optimization of pre-distributed entanglement allocation and static qubit placement, guided by circuit-aware training, consistently achieves the lowest execution times for benchmark circuits like QPE and QFT.
method: The problem is solved in three stages: allocating EPs under a budget, computing a static qubit-to-memory allocation, and finally executing the circuit while accounting for on-demand entanglement generation latency.
model_or_system: The system is a quantum network modeled as a graph connecting quantum computers (nodes) with quantum memories. Remote gates require EPs, and local connectivity is modeled by a coupling graph.
key_observables: Circuit execution time, total usage charge ($\Gamma$), and the number/latency of required entanglement pairs.
important_parameters: Pre-distribution budget ($K$), tradeoff parameter ($\lambda$), and network distance/freshness scores used in cost modeling.
main_assumptions: The analysis enforces a static qubit-allocation function ($\eta$) and assumes that consuming pre-distributed EPs incurs negligible online latency.
figures_summary: Figures compare execution time across different entanglement pair training methods (Greedy-C, SGD-C, Network-C) and qubit allocation algorithms (Greedy-$\eta$, exQAP-$\eta$, Annealing-$\eta$), showing the best results come from joint optimization.
paper_structure: The paper systematically tackles the DQC-PD problem by first defining the resource allocation (EPs), then the mapping (qubit allocation), and finally the execution protocol, culminating in comparative evaluations on benchmark circuits.
why_interesting: While focused on computation, the resource management aspects—modeling resource decay, optimizing resource placement, and minimizing latency—are highly relevant to building scalable quantum hardware architectures.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Quantum communication. (a) Teleportation and (b) Telegate. Dashed boxes are the network nodes; the initial (final) state of the qubits is at the top (bottom).

Fig. 2. Execution time of four benchmark families (QPE, QFT, Deutsch Jozsa, GHZ) under three pre-distributed EP trainers (Greedy-C, SGD-C, Network-C). Qubit allocation is fixed to Greedy-η. Results are shown for 10-wide qubit bins; the y-axis is logarithmic.

Fig. 3. Execution time of four benchmark families under three qubit-allocation algorithms (Greedy-η, exQAP-η, Annealing-η). The pre-distributed EP trainer is fixed to Greedy-C. Results are shown for 10-wide qubit bins; the y-axis is logarithmic.

Fig. 4. Execution time of four benchmark families under joint combinations of EP trainers and qubit-allocation methods. We report oracle-aligned training, i.e., C is trained using the same η-method applied at test time. Results are shown for 10-wide qubit bins; the y-axis is logarithmic.
